The son of an Irish mother and an Italian Civil War veteran, this Lower East Side native served four terms as New York's governor before becoming his party's 1928 presidential nominee — losing in a landslide to Herbert Hoover. Who was he?
Al Smith (December 30, 1873 - October 4, 1944) was an American politician who served as the 42nd governor of New York from 1919 to 1920 and again from 1923 to 1928.
This Russian chess grandmaster reigned as the 12th World Chess Champion from 1975 to 1985, later adding three more FIDE World Championship titles in the 1990s — who is he?
Anatoly Karpov (born May 23, 1951) is a Russian and former Soviet chess grandmaster, former World Chess Champion, and politician.
Appointed U.S. attorney by Ronald Reagan in 1982, this Republican later served two terms as governor of Arkansas before running for the 2024 presidential nomination — who is he?
Asa Hutchinson (born December 3, 1950) is an American attorney, businessman, and politician who served as the 46th governor of Arkansas from 2015 to 2023.

Battle of Zama was fought in 202 BC in what is now Tunisia between a Roman army commanded by Scipio Africanus and a Carthaginian army commanded by Hannibal.

Chris Hipkins (born 5 September 1978) is a New Zealand politician who has served as leader of the New Zealand Labour Party since January 2023 and leader of the Opposition since November 2023.
His reign may have fallen around the 9th century BC, and biblical scholars still debate whether his story is partly a political defense of his own dynasty — which king of Israel is it?
David (Biblical) was, originally, leader of the Tribe of Judah who became the second king of the united Kingdom of Israel, according to the Hebrew Bible and Old Testament.

Nicknamed 'Toby,' this barrister summed up his dream for a federated continent as 'a nation for a continent, and a continent for a nation' before becoming, in 1901, the very first to hold his nation's top office — who was he?
Edmund Barton (18 January 1849 - 7 January 1920) was an Australian politician, barrister and jurist who served as the first prime minister of Australia from 1901 to 1903.

Sometimes split into 'moral' and 'natural' forms — the latter covering disasters and illness — this broad concept denotes profound immorality and wickedness, though some philosophies deny it exists at all — what is it?
Evil is usually defined as profoundly immoral behavior, and it is related to acts that cause unnecessary pain and suffering to others.
Born in Punta Arenas to Croatian and Catalan stock, this left-wing leader rose from the 2011 student protests to become Chile's president in 2022 — without ever finishing his law degree. Who is he?
Gabriel Boric (born 11 February 1986) is a Chilean politician who served as President of Chile from 2022 to 2026.
At fifteen, this Swedish teenager began a solo school strike outside her country's parliament, sparking the worldwide Fridays for Future movement — who is she?
Greta Thunberg (born 3 January 2003) is a Swedish activist known for pressuring governments to address climate change and social issues.
This Indian politician has served multiple terms as Chief Minister of Jharkhand and leads the regional party Jharkhand Mukti Morcha — who is he?
Hemant Soren (born 10 August 1975) is an Indian politician who is serving as the 5th and current Chief Minister of Jharkhand since 4 July 2024 and the Leader of the House in Legislative Assembly.
After serving as the 29th chief of Turkey's General Staff, this general won a parliamentary seat for Kayseri in 2023 — who is he?
Hulusi Akar (born 12 March 1952) is a retired four-star Turkish Armed Forces general who served as the Minister of National Defense from 2018 to 2023.
Twin brother of Esau, this Torah patriarch tricked his aging father into giving him the blessing meant for his sibling, after already buying that sibling's birthright — who is he?
Jacob is the third Hebrew patriarch in Judaism and an important figure in the Abrahamic religions.
This Spanish lawyer and politician has twice served as president of FC Barcelona, first from 2003 to 2010, when the club won a record six trophies in a single year, and again since 2021 — who is he?
Joan Laporta (Catalan; born 29 June 1962) is a Spanish businessman, politician and president of FC Barcelona between 2003-2010 and 2021 onwards.
Born in 1995, this Nashville-area state representative was expelled in 2023 for leading a gun-control protest after the Covenant school shooting, then swiftly reinstated and reelected — who is he?
Justin Jones (Tennessee politician) (born August 25, 1995) is an American activist and politician from the state of Tennessee.
A German Schutzstaffel officer stationed in Vichy France during World War II, he became known as the 'Butcher of Lyon' for his torture of prisoners. Who was he?
Klaus Barbie (25 October 1913 - 25 September 1991) was a German officer of the Schutzstaffel and Sicherheitsdienst who worked in Vichy France during World War II.
Ranked third among the Ten Marshals of the People's Republic, which commander led the army into Beijing after winning the Liaoshen and Pingjin campaigns?
Lin Biao (5 December 1907 - 13 September 1971) was a Chinese military commander and politician.

After leading Mexico City's government for six years and introducing its Ecobici bike-share program, this politician went on to serve as Mexico's secretary of foreign affairs and later secretary of economy — who is he?
Marcelo Ebrard (born 10 October 1959) is a Mexican politician and internationalist who has served as the secretary of economy since 2024.

King Offa favored Tamworth and was crowned there, while nearby Repton held an important royal estate raided by the Great Heathen Army in 873 — which Anglo-Saxon kingdom of the English Midlands had no fixed capital?
Mercia was an early medieval English kingdom, one of the seven kingdoms of the Anglo-Saxon period.
This American activist became internationally known in the late 1990s after a US president admitted to an affair with her during her time as a White House intern — who is she?
Monica Lewinsky (born July 23, 1973) is an American activist.
He won a rigged 1967 election to become president of South Vietnam, then resigned and fled to Taipei days before the fall of Saigon — who is he?
Nguyễn Văn Thiệu (5 April 1923 - 29 September 2001) was a South Vietnamese military officer and politician who was the president of South Vietnam from 1967 to 1975.

Regarded as perhaps Nazi Germany's most extreme executioner, this German officer commanded a notorious penal brigade of the Waffen-SS responsible for some of World War II's worst atrocities — who was he?

This French politician served three times as Prime Minister — twice under the Third Republic and once under Vichy France — before being executed for treason as a Nazi collaborator after the war — who is he?
Pierre Laval (28 June 1883 - 15 October 1945) was a French politician.

Before he took the throne, this fifth ruler of Egypt's Twentieth Dynasty was a prince named Amunherkhepeshef who served as royal scribe and cavalry general — which eight-year reign of the 12th century BC is it?
Ramesses VI (sometimes written Ramses or Rameses, also known under his princely name of Amenherkhepshef C) was the fifth ruler of the Twentieth Dynasty of Egypt.
Dubbed the "Queen of Drag," this entertainer has hauled in 14 Primetime Emmys plus a Tony and even a Guinness World Records title — who is it?
RuPaul (born November 17, 1960) is an American drag queen, television host, singer, producer, writer, and actor.

Despite lacking staff officer training, this SS general — once Hitler's chauffeur — was assessed by a fellow commander as 'decent but stupid,' yet still reached the top command rank of the Waffen-SS — who is he?
Sepp Dietrich (28 May 1892 - 21 April 1966) was a German general, politician and war criminal in the Schutzstaffel (SS) during the Nazi era.
On a night in 1983, this Soviet duty officer saw his early-warning system report a US missile launch — and chose to call it a false alarm rather than report an attack. Who is it?
Stanislav Petrov (7 September 1939 - 19 May 2017) was a Russian lieutenant colonel of the Soviet Air Defence Forces who played a key role in the 1983 Soviet nuclear false alarm incident.

His parochial knack for haranguing federal leaders won South Australia a wildly disproportionate share of national funding — and the longest unbroken term of any elected leader in Australian history. Who was this premier?
Thomas Playford IV (5 July 1896 - 16 June 1981) was an Australian politician from the state of South Australia.
A sub-orbital spaceflight participant as well as an undersea explorer, he co-founded a private equity firm and reached the poles and Seven Summits before conquering the ocean floor. Who is he?
Victor Vescovo (born February 10, 1966) is an American private equity investor, retired naval officer, sub-orbital spaceflight participant, and undersea explorer.
This career diplomat briefly served as acting U.S. secretary of state for a single day in 2009, and later led the CIA throughout the Biden administration — who is he?

William J. Burns (diplomat) (born April 11, 1956) is an American diplomat who served as the 8th director of the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) during the Biden administration from March 19, 2021 to January 20, 2025.

Ziaur Rahman (19 January 1936 - 30 May 1981) was a Bangladeshi military leader and politician who served as the sixth president of Bangladesh from 1977 until his assassination in 1981.
This Polish lawyer and human rights activist served as the country's 7th Ombudsman from 2015 to 2021 before becoming Minister of Justice from 2023 to 2025 — who is he?

Adam Bodnar: Polish human rights activist and ombudsman. Adam Piotr Bodnar (born 6 January 1977) is a Polish lawyer, educator, human rights activist and politician who served as Minister of Justice from 2023 to 2025.
A private first class with Easy Company's 506th Parachute Infantry in World War II, this soldier jumped with the Airborne again in Korea, twice earning decorations for gallantry — who is he?
Albert Blithe: United States Army soldier.

Almanzor: Andalusian military leader and statesman (c. 938–1002)
Serving as Governor of Jakarta before running for president in 2024, this Indonesian politician founded a program that sends university graduates to teach for a year nationwide — who is he?

A close aide to Egyptian presidents Nasser and Sadat, this official was allegedly a Mossad spy who fed Israel intelligence before the Yom Kippur War, then died mysteriously falling from a London balcony in 2007 — who was he?
Ashraf Marwan: Egyptian businessman and spy (1944–2007)
This Indian engineer-turned-politician served as Karnataka's 17th chief minister from 2021 to 2023 before becoming a Lok Sabha MP for Haveri — who is he?
Basavaraj Bommai: 23rd Chief Minister of Karnataka from 2021 to 2023. In July 2022, Bommai became only the second person from BJP to complete one year as chief minister of the state.

Lasting three days in September 2004, this hostage crisis in North Ossetia, Russia, took over 1,100 captives including 777 children and is considered history's deadliest attack on an educational institution — which crisis?
Beslan school siege: 2004 Russian hostage crisis and massacre.
Lasting from 1858 to 1947, this era of Crown rule over the Indian subcontinent blended directly governed provinces with princely states under British paramountcy. What was it?
British Raj: 1858–1947 Crown colonial rule in India.

Identified chiefly by a shared family of Indo-European languages, this collection of ancient peoples included the Gauls, the Britons and Picts of Britain and Ireland, and the Galatians of Anatolia — who were they?
Celts: Collection of indo-European peoples sharing Celtic languages and cultural practices.
This Costa Rican diplomat took over UN climate negotiations six months after the failed Copenhagen summit and helped broker the 2015 Paris Agreement — who is she?

This Renaissance-era Florentine banker used his fortune to become the city's de facto first ruler, commissioning a bronze statue considered the first freestanding nude male sculpture since antiquity — who was he?
Cosimo de' Medici: Lord of Florence from 1434 to 1464.

The longest-serving prime minister of Iceland and former mayor of Reykjavík, he later chaired the Central Bank — and the 2008 financial crisis sparked loud public demands for his resignation. Who was he?

Born into a wealthy New York family and educated at the University of Pennsylvania, this real estate mogul became the 47th president after a career of branded towers, hotels, casinos, and side ventures — who is he?
Donald Trump: President of the United States (2017–2021; since 2025)
From the French word for 'equal,' this school of political philosophy holds that all humans share the same fundamental worth and deserve equal rights under the law. What is it called?
Egalitarianism: School of thought favoring equality for all people.
In Greek mythology, this goddess of strife started a quarrel among Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite that led to the Judgement of Paris and, ultimately, the Trojan War — who is she?
Eris (mythology): Greek goddess of strife and discord. All of Eris' children are little more than allegorizations of the meanings of their names, with virtually no other identity.
The last man ever promoted to Field Marshal in the German military during World War II, this commander became notorious among his own troops for his brutal treatment of deserters — who was he?

French Consulate: Government of France from 1799 to 1804.
Becoming the first openly LGBTQ Republican elected to Congress as a freshman, this New York representative was expelled within a year after much of his biography proved fabricated — who is he?
George Santos: American politician and convicted felon (born 1988)
Trapped by an anticyclone and windless conditions in December 1952, this coal-fueled pollution event over England's capital killed an estimated 4,000 people in less than a week — what was it called?
Great Smog of London: 1952 air pollution event. It lasted from Friday, 5 December to Tuesday, 9 December 1952, then dispersed quickly when the weather changed.

A general, poet, and inventor of the Song dynasty, this commander was famed for winning battles against larger forces — and was said to have ended his career covered in scars with only four fingers left on his hands. Who was he?

This Welsh privateer raided Spanish settlements from his Port Royal base, then used the plunder to buy three Jamaican sugar plantations and eventually became the island's lieutenant governor — who was he?
Henry Morgan: Welsh privateer, politician in Jamaica (1635–1688)
Formed by the 1736 marriage of a French duke to Maria Theresa of Austria, this dynasty merged two royal lines, inheriting through the mother's family and the father's — which dynasty?
House of Habsburg-Lorraine: Austrian imperial dynasty.
This Ukrainian politician fled to Russia in 2022 and publicly backed its invasion of Ukraine, leading parliament to strip his mandate and Ukrainian courts to convict him of treason — who was he?
Educated at Al-Azhar and later a preacher in his native Jableh, this early-20th-century leader fought against French rule in Syria and British rule in Palestine — who was he?
Izz ad-Din al-Qassam: Syrian Muslim preacher (1882–1935)
After leading Taiwan's Environmental Protection Administration, this media personality co-founded the pro-unification New Party and ran for vice president on the KMT ticket in 2024 — who is he?
Jaw Shaw-kong: Taiwanese media personality and politician.
This North Carolina senator ran as the Democratic vice-presidential nominee alongside Kerry in 2004, after twice seeking his party's presidential nomination — who was he?
John Edwards: American lawyer and politician (born 1953)
Born in Roman exile and grandson of Alfonso XIII, this royal reigned over Spain from 1975 until abdicating in 2014, after which the press dubbed him the rey emérito — who is he?
Juan Carlos I: King of Spain from 1975 to 2014. In Spain, since his abdication, Juan Carlos has usually been referred to as the rey emérito ('king emeritus') by the press.

Emerging from the fragmentation of the Golden Horde around 1465, this Central Asian nomadic state eventually stretched from the Caspian and Aral seas to the Ural Mountains under Kasym Khan — what was it?
Kazakh Khanate: 1465–1847 Turkic state in Central Asia.
Roughly 100,000 prospectors stampeded toward Canada's Yukon after an 1896 strike, most braving the brutal Chilkoot or White Pass trails — a frenzy later immortalized in films and photographs as what?
Klondike Gold Rush: 1896–1899 migration to Yukon, Canada.
This political ideology calls for a revolutionary vanguard party to lead a "dictatorship of the proletariat" as the prelude to communism — what is it named for its Russian architect?
Leninism: Political theory developed by Vladimir Lenin.

Crowned in 844 and co-ruling with his father Lothair I until 855, this Carolingian emperor adopted the title 'emperor of the Romans' after conquering Bari in 871 — straining ties with Byzantium. Who was he?
Louis II of Italy: Ruler of the Carolingian Empire from 844 to 875.
This Northern Irish peace activist co-founded a movement seeking a peaceful end to the Troubles, sharing the 1976 Nobel Peace Prize with Betty Williams — who is she?
Mairead Maguire: Northern Irish peace activist (born 1944)
Before becoming Italy's prime minister in 2021, this economist spent eight years as president of the European Central Bank — who is he?
Mario Draghi: Prime Minister of Italy from 2021 to 2022.
Nicknamed 'The Restorer' after reuniting a fractured empire in 1413 following a civil war among brothers, this Ottoman sultan lost a naval battle to Venice off Gallipoli in 1416 — who was he?
Mehmed I: Sultan of the Ottoman Empire from 1413 to 1421.
This retired military officer studied law in Rangoon, led the Tatmadaw from 2011, and has ruled his country since seizing power in a February 2021 coup — who is he?
Min Aung Hlaing: Burmese politician and military officer (born 1956)
This young Arab commander, serving the Umayyad Caliphate, captured the region of Sindh around 712, marking the start of Muslim rule in South Asia — who is he?
Muhammad ibn al-Qasim: Umayyad general and governor of Sindh (695–715)
Before becoming President of India in 1977, this politician had been chief minister of Andhra Pradesh and a two-time Speaker of the Lok Sabha — who is it?
Neelam Sanjiva Reddy: President of India from 1977 to 1982.
The younger son of Neferirkare Kakai and Queen Khentkaus II, this sixth ruler of Egypt's Fifth Dynasty likely took the throne after his short-lived brother Neferefre. Which Old Kingdom king was he?
Nyuserre Ini: Ancient Egyptian pharaoh of the Fifth Dynasty.

One of the Three Kingdoms of Korea alongside Goguryeo and Silla, this kingdom in the southwest had the largest population of the three and was founded by Onjo near present-day Seoul. Which kingdom was it?
Paekche: Ancient Korean kingdom (18 BCE – 660 CE)
Considered the most influential artist of the Flemish Baroque, this painter and diplomat was known for dramatic, sensual compositions and designs for tapestry workshops — who is he?
Peter Paul Rubens: Flemish artist and diplomat (1577–1640)
Married to King George V's third son and living to age 102, she became the British royal family's longest-lived member — who was she?
Princess Alice, Duchess of Gloucester: Member of the British royal family (1901–2004)
An NKVD agent who assassinated Leon Trotsky in Mexico City with an ice axe in 1940, he served nearly 20 years in prison — then emerged to be honored as a Hero of the Soviet Union. Who was he?
Ramón Mercader: Assassin of Leon Trotsky (1913–1978)
This American oceanographer discovered the wrecks of the Titanic, the Bismarck, and the USS Yorktown, and once said finding hydrothermal vents beat finding that famous ocean liner — who is he?
Robert Ballard: Retired US Navy officer and professor of oceanography (born 1942)
A Keio University graduate who entered Japan's National Diet in 1963, this politician served as prime minister from 1996 to 1998 before resigning after a coalition election defeat — who is he?

Ryutaro Hashimoto: Prime Minister of Japan from 1996 to 1998. Ryutaro Hashimoto (橋本 龍太郎, Hashimoto Ryūtarō; 29 July 1937 – 1 July 2006) was a Japanese politician who served as prime minister of Japan from 1996 to 1998.
A philosopher who held a chair in comparative religion at Calcutta before entering public life, this scholar rose from Vice President to President of India in 1962 — who was he?
Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan: President of India from 1962 to 1967. Radhakrishnan's philosophy was grounded in Advaita Vedanta, reinterpreting this tradition for a contemporary understanding.
In 1902, this Indian princely ruler issued one of India's earliest affirmative-action orders, reserving half of government jobs and education for backward classes — who was he?
Shahu of Kolhapur: Indian ruler and social reformer (1894 to 1922)

Sino-Indian War: 1962 war between China and India. It was a military escalation of the Sino-Indian border dispute.
A British barrister who twice held the post of Home Secretary in 2022, this MP for Fareham made headlines in January 2026 by defecting from the Conservatives to Reform UK — who is she?
The son of Odysseus and Penelope, this young man sailed to Pylos and Sparta seeking news of his father, then helped slay the suitors back home in Ithaca — who is he?
Telemachus: Mythological son of Odysseus. When Telemachus reached manhood, he visited Pylos and Sparta in search of his wandering father.
Tamerlane, founder of the Timurid Empire, holds what distinction as a commander?
He was never defeated in battle

This liberal religious tradition has no single creed, instead uniting congregations through shared covenants centered on love and pluralistic worship, drawing on everything from Christianity to Buddhism — which faith tradition?
Unitarian Universalism: Non-creedal liberal religious movement.

Ruling for just eight months during the chaotic Year of the Four Emperors, this Roman ruler took the honorific Germanicus instead of Caesar and tried to boost his popularity by imitating the still-beloved Nero — who was he?
This unofficial coalition of countries officially allied with the United States during the Cold War stood in opposition to the Soviet Union and the Warsaw Pact — what was this group called?
Western Bloc: Group of states aligned with the United States during the Cold War. The name "Western Bloc" emerged in response to and as the antithesis of its communist counterpart, the Eastern Bloc.
This 7th-century Chinese Buddhist monk journeyed to the Indian subcontinent from 629 to 645 CE and brought back more than 650 Sanskrit texts to translate — who is he?
Xuanzang: Chinese Buddhist monk and scholar (602–664)
Emerging in late-19th-century Europe in reaction to antisemitism and led by Theodor Herzl, this nationalist movement sought a Jewish homeland in Palestine — what is it?
Zionism: Jewish nationalist movement. The arrival of Zionist settlers in Palestine during this period is widely seen as marking the start of the Israeli–Palestinian conflict.

Fortran (founded 1957) is the earliest of the four.

MATLAB (founded 1984) is the earliest of the four. MATLAB (Matrix Laboratory) is a proprietary multi-paradigm programming language and numeric computing environment developed by MathWorks.
Which of these four is a physicist?
Who among these is a chemist?
Stephanie Kwolek is a chemist. Stephanie Louise Kwolek (July 31, 1923 – June 18, 2014) was a Polish-American chemist known for inventing Kevlar (poly-paraphenylene terephthalamide).
What is the atomic number of Tennessine?
Tennessine is a synthetic element; it has symbol Ts and atomic number 117.
What is the atomic number of Astatine?
Astatine is a chemical element; it has symbol At and atomic number 85.
In what year did Tomitaro Makino die?
Tomitaro Makino (牧野 富太郎, Makino Tomitarō; 24 April 1862 – 18 January 1957) was a pioneer Japanese botanist noted for his taxonomic work.
In what year was Aluminium discovered?
Aluminium (the Commonwealth and preferred IUPAC name) or aluminum (North American English) is a chemical element; it has symbol Al and atomic number 13.
Which company manufactures Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird?
Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird: Skunk Works. The SR-71 was developed in the 1960s as a black project by Lockheed's Skunk Works division.
Cro-Magnon: France. Cro-Magnons produced Upper Palaeolithic cultures, the first major one being the Aurignacian, which was succeeded by the Gravettian by 30,000 years ago.
Who is credited with discovering Tucana?
Tucana: Petrus Plancius. Tucana (The Toucan) is a constellation in the southern sky, named after the toucan, a South American bird.
Who is credited with discovering Cro-Magnon?
Cro-Magnon: Louis Lartet. Cro-Magnons produced Upper Palaeolithic cultures, the first major one being the Aurignacian, which was succeeded by the Gravettian by 30,000 years ago.
Who is credited with discovering Makemake?
Makemake: Michael E. Brown. Makemake (minor-planet number 136472) is a dwarf planet orbiting the Sun in the Kuiper belt, a disc of icy bodies beyond the orbit of Neptune.
Found on every continent except Antarctica, this family of hook-billed raptors includes buzzards, vultures, and kites across 75 genera — which family is this?
Accipitridae is one of the four families within the order Accipitriformes, and is a family of small to large birds of prey with strongly hooked bills and variable morphology based on diet.
A close relative of the peach in the genus Prunus, this drupe's seed isn't a true nut and can be "blanched" by softening its skin in hot water before peeling — what is it?
This British-American theoretical physicist at the University of Illinois reshaped our understanding of superfluid helium, work crowned by the 2003 Nobel Prize in Physics — who was he?
Anthony Leggett (26 March 1938 - 8 March 2026) was a British-American theoretical physicist and professor at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (UIUC).
This common long-term inflammatory airway disease causes wheezing, coughing, and shortness of breath that can flare into sudden attacks triggered by allergens or pollen. What condition is it?
Asthma is a common long-term inflammatory disease of the airways. It is characterized by variable and recurring symptoms and reduced lung function.
Strawberries, blackcurrants and blueberries all count in the kitchen sense — though botanists would object, since the culinary meaning of this word differs from the scientific one. What word?
Berry is a small, pulpy, and often edible fruit.

Developed in Germany from the Old English Bulldog and the now-extinct Bullenbeisser, this medium-to-large mastiff-type dog breed is known for its square muzzle, underbite, and powerful bite — name the breed?
Boxer (dog breed) is a medium to large, short-haired dog breed of mastiff-type, developed in Germany.
The leaves and buds of this evergreen shrub, when processed differently, yield green, black, oolong, white, and yellow varieties of the world's most popular hot beverage — what's the species?
Camellia sinensis is a species of evergreen shrub or small tree in the flowering plant family Theaceae.
In calculus, this formula lets you find the derivative of a composed function h(x) = z(y(x)) using the derivatives of z and y separately — what is it called?
Chain rule is a formula that expresses the derivative of the composition of two differentiable functions z and y in terms of the derivatives of z and y.
Living in a symbiotic partnership with sea anemones that shelter them from predators, these Indo-Pacific reef fish live in groups led by a dominant breeding female. What fish are they?
Clownfish (genus Amphiprion) are saltwater fish found in the warm and tropical waters of the Indo-Pacific.
Which genus of passerine birds, whose Latin name literally means 'raven,' includes about 46 species commonly known as crows, ravens, and rooks?
Corvus is a widely distributed genus of passerine birds ranging from medium-sized to large-sized in the family Corvidae.
Used to treat ADHD and narcolepsy, this 'right-handed' mirror-image form of a stimulant molecule is also misused to boost cognitive and athletic performance — what is it?
Dextroamphetamine is a central nervous system (CNS) stimulant and enantiomer of amphetamine that is used in the treatment of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and narcolepsy.
Long used in traditional Indigenous medicine, this prairie-dwelling genus of purple daisy relatives gets its name from a Greek word meaning 'hedgehog' — what plant is it?
Echinacea is a genus of herbaceous flowering plants in the daisy family.

Discovered in January 2005 by a Palomar Observatory team and named after a Greco-Roman goddess of strife, this trans-Neptunian object is the most massive known dwarf planet in the solar system — which one?
Eris (dwarf planet) (minor-planet number 136199) is the most massive and second-largest known dwarf planet in the Solar System.
With over two hundred species across fifty genera, this bird family includes canaries, siskins, redpolls, grosbeaks, and the Hawaiian honeycreepers — which family of seed-eating passerines?
Finch are small to medium-sized passerine birds in the family Fringillidae.
Caused by abnormalities in the genome, this category of health problem may arise from a single faulty gene, many genes, or a chromosome abnormality — what is the general term?
Genetic disorder is a health problem caused by one or more abnormalities in the genome.
Nicknamed the 'benevolent dictator for life' of the language he invented, this Dutch programmer relinquished that title in July 2018. Who is he?
Guido van Rossum (born 31 January 1956) is a Dutch programmer.
This genus of the mallow family includes several hundred species prized for their large, showy blooms, and is sometimes known by the alternate name rose mallow — name the genus?
Hibiscus is a genus of common flowering plants in the mallow family, Malvaceae.
Prized in folk medicine as an antiseptic and expectorant, this Lamiaceae shrub grows wild from Southern Europe to the Caspian Sea area — which plant is it?
Hyssopus officinalis is a shrub in the Lamiaceae or mint family native to Southern Europe, the Middle East, and the region surrounding the Caspian Sea.
This Canadian-American physical educator invented an entire sport, wrote its original rule book after moving to the United States, and founded the University of Kansas's program in 1898 — who is he?
James Naismith (November 6, 1861 - November 28, 1939) was a Canadian-American physical educator, physician, Christian chaplain, and sports coach, best known as the inventor of the game of basketball.
Cousin to the wallaby and wallaroo in the family Macropodidae, this Australian marsupial's biggest member is the red one. What is it?
Kangaroo are marsupials from the subfamily Macropodinae (macropods, meaning "large foot").

Which citrus-scented perennial herb in the mint family, whose genus name Melissa comes from the Greek for 'honey bee,' is naturalized worldwide after originating in the Mediterranean and Central Asia?
Lemon balm (Melissa officinalis) is a perennial herbaceous plant in the mint family.
This Berkeley professor upended classical logic by proposing 'fuzzy' mathematics — fuzzy sets, fuzzy logic, fuzzy control, and more — who was he?

Lotfi A. Zadeh (4 February 1921 - 6 September 2017) was a mathematician, computer scientist, electrical engineer, artificial intelligence researcher, and professor of computer science at the University of California, Berkeley.
Sharing the 1963 Nobel Prize in Physics for work on nuclear shell structure, this German-American theorist became only the second woman ever to win that prize, after Marie Curie — who was she?
Maria Goeppert Mayer (ne Goppert; June 28, 1906 - February 20, 1972) was a German-American theoretical physicist who shared the 1963 Nobel Prize in Physics with J. Hans D. Jensen.
This branch of economics studies how individuals and firms allocate scarce resources within individual markets, as opposed to the economy as a whole — what field is it?

Microeconomics is a branch of economics that studies the behavior of individuals and firms in making decisions regarding the allocation of scarce resources and the interactions among these individuals and firms.
This semiaquatic rodent can stay submerged for up to seventeen minutes, propelled mainly by its webbed hind feet while its long, scaly tail helps steer — what animal is it?
Muskrat (Ondatra zibethicus) is a medium-sized semiaquatic rodent.
A reddish-brown gas that's a key step in making nitric acid for fertilizer, it also seeps into homes from gas-stove cooking and harms indoor air — which compound, formula NO2?
Nitrogen dioxide is a chemical compound with the formula NO2.

This group of middle-ear inflammations includes a painful acute infection that makes young children tug at their ears, plus a quieter form defined by non-infectious fluid lingering for weeks. What is the condition?
Otitis media is a group of inflammatory diseases of the middle ear.
Built for the sea, it sports a spiny tongue and powerful jaws to grip slippery fish, then swallows them whole mid-swim. Which animal splits its life half on land, half in the water?
Penguin are a group of flightless semi-aquatic sea birds which live almost exclusively in the Southern Hemisphere.
Native to South America and the most economically important member of the Bromeliaceae family, this tropical 'multiple fruit' became a 17th-century European symbol of luxury — what is it?
Pineapple (Ananas comosus) is a tropical plant with an edible fruit; it is the most economically significant plant in the family Bromeliaceae.

This male sexual dysfunction occurs when orgasm happens very soon after minimal sexual stimulation, with medical experts generally setting the threshold at around one minute — what's this condition called?

Premature ejaculation (PE) is a male sexual dysfunction that occurs when a male expels semen (and most likely experiences orgasm) soon after beginning sexual activity, and with minimal penile stimulation.
This colorless, odorless radioactive noble gas has the atomic number 86, and its longest-lived isotope has a half-life of under four days — name the element?
Radon is a chemical element; it has symbol Rn and atomic number 86.
Known by the common name 'dog rose,' this climbing wild rose species is native across Europe and stretches into northwest Africa and western Asia — which species?
Rosa canina is a variable climbing, wild rose species native to Europe, northwest Africa, and western Asia.

Seven living species make up this group of ocean-dwelling reptiles, five of which are threatened with extinction — one species, found only near Australia, Papua New Guinea, and Indonesia, is not — name this group?
Sea turtle (superfamily Chelonioidea), sometimes called marine turtles, are reptiles of the order Testudines and of the suborder Cryptodira.
Whether on land, in fresh water, or in the sea, this gastropod earns its name from a coiled shell roomy enough to fully retract into — what is it?
Snail is a shelled gastropod. The name is most often applied to land snails, terrestrial pulmonate gastropod molluscs.
This group of cartilaginous fish spans eleven families and roughly 220 species, from tiny river-dwellers to giant manta and devil rays — what group of fish is it?
Stingray are a group of rays, a type of cartilaginous fish.
This fibrous connective tissue connects muscle to bone, unlike its cousin which connects bone to bone, and numbers about 4,000 throughout the adult human body — what is it?
Tendon is a tough band of dense fibrous connective tissue that connects muscle to bone.
Caused by superantigens from staph or strep bacteria, this condition brings fever, a sunburn-like rash, and peeling skin, and has been tied to absorbent tampon use — which condition?
Toxic shock syndrome (TSS) is a condition caused by bacterial toxins.
This abnormal enlargement of the vein network draining the testicles is the most common correctable cause of male infertility, found in over a third of men with the condition. Name it?
Varicocele is an abnormal enlargement of the pampiniform venous plexus in the scrotum.
This biological process unfolds in predictable phases — hemostasis, inflammation, cell proliferation, and tissue remodeling — to replace damaged skin after the barrier is broken. What is it?
Wound healing refers to a living organism's replacement of destroyed or damaged tissue by newly produced tissue.
The simplest alkyne, this colorless gas packs all four of its atoms into one straight line thanks to a carbon-carbon triple bond, and fuels welding torches — which compound is it?
First nominated by Ronald Reagan in 1987 and reappointed every four years until 2006, this soft-spoken economist logged the second-longest tenure ever as chairman of the Federal Reserve — who was he?
Alan Greenspan: American economist and financial advisor (born 1926)

Nicknamed 'lazy eye,' this childhood vision disorder occurs when the brain favors one eye over the other, and correcting the underlying cause doesn't restore sight right away — what is this condition?
Amblyopia: Failure of the brain to process input from one eye.
Comprising over 22,000 species including ragworms, earthworms, and leeches, this phylum of segmented worms use parapodia to move — what is it?
Annelid: Phylum of segmented worms. The basic annelid form consists of multiple segments called metameres.

Known only from fragmentary remains including vertebrae and a giant femur first found by a farmer in 1987, this titanosaur may be the largest land animal ever discovered, stretching up to 35 meters — which genus?
Argentinosaurus: Late Cretaceous giant sauropod dinosaur genus.
The famous AL 288-1 skeleton nicknamed 'Lucy,' unearthed in Ethiopia's Afar region, belongs to which extinct East African hominin species that lived roughly 3.9 to 2.9 million years ago?
Australopithecus afarensis: Extinct hominid from the Pliocene of East Africa.
This inflammatory condition causes recurring, painful mouth sores along with eye inflammation and arthritis, and is diagnosed after at least three sore outbreaks in a year — which condition?
Behçet's disease: Inflammatory disorder. Behçet's disease or Behçet's syndrome (BD; sometimes written Behcet) is a type of inflammatory disorder which affects multiple parts of the body.
Rich in vitamin C and polyphenols, this deciduous shrub's glossy dark berries are cooked into jams and syrups or fermented into cassis — what is it?
Blackcurrant: Species of flowering plant in the gooseberry family Grossulariaceae.

This infraorder of decapod crustaceans tucks a stubby tail-like abdomen under a hard shell and ends its front pair of legs in pincers — over 1.5 million tonnes of them are eaten by humans yearly. What group is it?
Brachyura: Crustacean. The true crabs are the largest of the crab decapod groups with carcinised body forms.
A cole crop related to broccoli, cauliflower and Brussels sprouts, the heaviest recorded head of this leafy vegetable weighed nearly 138 pounds — what is it?
Cabbage: Leafy vegetable in the flowering plant family Brassicaceae.

Time called her the "literary godmother" to Paris's Lost Generation, and her Black Sun Press printed early Hemingway and Henry Miller — but she also patented the first successful modern bra. Who was she?
Usually arising from damage to the developing brain before birth, this group of childhood movement disorders causes stiff or weak muscles, tremors, and poor coordination — what condition?
Cerebral palsy: Movement disorders that appear in early childhood.
Every animal in this group shares five telltale traits — including a notochord, pharyngeal slits, and a tail that extends past the anus — at some stage of life; which of these belongs to that phylum?
Chordate: Phylum of animals having a dorsal nerve cord.
This genus of demersal fish, named by Linnaeus in 1758, includes an Atlantic and a Pacific species prized for their mild flavor and flaky white flesh — what fish is it?
Cod: Common name for several fish, but mainly the demersal genus Gadus.
With a long hooked bill and webbing between all four toes, this fish-eating aquatic bird family includes the 'great' species commonly seen around Britain and Ireland — what are they called?
Cormorant: Family of aquatic birds. The common names "cormorant" and "shag" have been assigned to different species in the family somewhat haphazardly.
Native to South and Southeast Asia and often sold as fresh stems, this tropical plant known as West Indian lemon grass can't survive a frost — what is it?
A fluorinated glucocorticoid, this medication treats everything from severe allergies and asthma to brain swelling and croup, and is given to ease preterm-labor outcomes — what is it?
Dexamethasone: Corticosteroid medication. The effects of dexamethasone are frequently seen within a day and last for about three days.
Also called Trisomy 21, this condition is caused by an extra copy of a single chromosome and grows more likely with a mother's age — from under 0.1% at 20 to about 3% at 45. What is it?
This unit of energy equals the kinetic energy a single electron gains while crossing an electric potential difference of one volt — what is it called?
Sometimes abbreviated ETM, this antibiotic treats everything from respiratory infections to syphilis and is the eye ointment routinely dabbed on newborns to prevent eye infections. What is it?
Erythromycin: Antibiotic medication. Erythromycin (sometimes abbreviated ETM in reports) is an antibiotic used for the treatment of a number of bacterial infections.
Native to the Iberian Peninsula and introduced to hundreds of locations worldwide, this grassland herbivore digs extensive burrow networks called warrens — what is it?
This genus of over 200 stinging insect species, Solenopsis, includes 'ginger' and 'tropical' varieties named for their painful bite and reddish coloring — what are they commonly called?
Fire ant: Genus of red ants.
A French economist who gave up accounting to lecture across France, he founded peace societies and the Inter-Parliamentary Union before sharing the very first Nobel Peace Prize in 1901. Who was he?
Frédéric Passy: French economist and pacifist (1822–1912)
Ranging from Baja California to Japan's coast, this cephalopod is the largest of its kind on Earth and a common aquarium favorite — which creature?
Giant Pacific octopus: Species of cephalopod. It can be found from the intertidal zone down to 2,000 m (6,600 ft), and is best-adapted to colder, oxygen- and nutrient-rich waters.
The seeds of five plants in this family, including rice, wheat, maize, barley, and sugar cane, cover 46% of the world's farmland — what group of plants is this?
Grass: Collective name for three families of plants.
The best-known of these rodents is the golden or Syrian species, though dwarf varieties like Campbell's and the Roborovski are popular too — what small pet is this?
Its name Greek for 'different wings,' this insect suborder of about 40,000 species is the group most consistently termed 'true bugs' within Hemiptera — which group is it?
Heteroptera: Suborder of true bugs. The name "Heteroptera" is used in two very different ways in modern classifications.
Also known as dihydrocodeinone, this semi-synthetic opioid is often combined with acetaminophen or ibuprofen for pain and is sold alone as an extended-release drug called Zohydro ER — what is it?
Hydrocodone: Opioid drug used in pain relief.
This contagious bacterial skin infection — usually from Staph or Strep — most often shows up as yellowish crusts on the face, arms or legs. What's it called?

This Scottish physicist's equations unified electricity, magnetism, and light into a single theory — the second great unification in physics after Newton's — while also helping found statistical mechanics — who is he?
James Clerk Maxwell: Scottish physicist and mathematician (1831–1879)
Struggling with a morphine addiction from a Civil War saber wound, this pharmacist and chemist developed a coca-and-caffeine beverage in 1886 that became Coca-Cola — who is he?
John Stith Pemberton: American pharmacist, inventor of Coca-Cola (1831–1888)
A biologist and botanist married four times — her last husband directed the Manhattan Project's Los Alamos lab — she was played by Emily Blunt in a 2023 film. Who was she?
Its lens-shaped seeds, usually two to a pod, are split and simmered into the dal that's a staple across the Indian subcontinent — which legume?
Lentil: Species of plant with edible seeds.

Providing the USAF with intercontinental strategic airlift for oversized cargo, this jumbo transport is among the largest military aircraft ever built and shares lineage with the smaller Starlifter — what is it?
Lockheed C-5 Galaxy: American heavy military transport aircraft.

With a fruiting body resembling an open umbrella, this fungus often grows in fairy rings across Eurasian pastures and is prized as a good edible despite resembling toxic look-alikes — what's its scientific name?
Macrolepiota procera: Species of fungus. Macrolepiota procera, the parasol mushroom, is a basidiomycete fungus with a large, prominent fruiting body resembling a parasol.
In 2014 this Stanford mathematician became the first woman and first Iranian to win the Fields Medal, honored for her work on the geometry of Riemann surfaces — who was she?
Patented in 1922 and later marketed as Novalgin or Analgin, this painkiller's sale is restricted in some countries due to a rare blood-cell risk called agranulocytosis — what is it?
Metamizole: Medication. Metamizole or dipyrone is a painkiller, spasm reliever, and fever reliever drug.
Marketed under names like Rogaine and Loniten, this medication treats high blood pressure but is best known over-the-counter for combating hair loss — what's the drug?
Minoxidil: Medication to treat high blood pressure and alopecia.
This contagious, vaccine-preventable viral disease is best known for causing painful swelling of the glands beside the jaw — its hallmark symptom. What is it?
Mumps: Human disease caused by paramyxovirus.
Commonly called horsehair worms, these parasitoid animals get their nickname from the Gordian knot because of how they tangle themselves up — what phylum is this?

Nematomorpha: Phylum of parasitoid animals; horsehair worms. The adult worms are free-living, but the larvae are parasitic on arthropods, such as beetles, cockroaches, mantises, orthopterans, and crustaceans.
This facial organ houses the nares, connects to the humidity-regulating paranasal sinuses, and serves as an alternate airway for nursing infants — which body part?
Nose: Organ that smells and facilitates breathing.
Sold under the brand name Tamiflu, this oral antiviral is recommended for high-risk patients within 48 hours of their first flu symptoms. What drug is it?
Oseltamivir: Antiviral medication used against influenza.
Believed to have originated in Sardinia and first cultivated in Britain in 1548, which herb is often used simply as a garnish today?
Parsley: Species of flowering plant in the celery family Apiaceae cultivated as an herb.
Dubbed 'the champion of management as a serious discipline,' this Austrian-American writer popularized the concept of management by objectives — who is he?
Peter Drucker: American management consultant and author (1909–2005)
Known as the Scots pine in Britain, this Eurasian conifer is identifiable by its blue-green needles and orange-red bark — which species?
Pinus sylvestris: Species of conifer. Pinus sylvestris is a species of tree in the pine family Pinaceae that is native to Eurasia.
Also known as niter or saltpeter, this compound is a key ingredient of traditional gunpowder and gives cured meats their reddish color — what is it?
Potassium nitrate: Chemical compound. Potassium nitrate is a chemical compound with a sharp, salty, bitter taste and the chemical formula KNO3.
Fossils of this genus, found in Germany's Solnhofen limestone, mark the first pterosaur ever identified as a flying reptile — which genus?
Pterodactylus: Genus of pterodactyloid pterosaur from the Late Jurassic.
Belonging to the genus Corvus and distinguished from its close relatives mainly by size, the largest species in this bird category are also the largest of all perching birds — which bird?
Raven: Index of animals with the same common name.
This Israeli-American mathematician shared the 2005 Nobel in Economics with Thomas Schelling for illuminating conflict and cooperation through game theory — who is he?
Caused by bacteria in the Salmonella genus, this common form of food poisoning brings diarrhea, fever, and cramps within 12 to 36 hours of eating contaminated food — what is it called?
Salmonellosis: Infection caused by Salmonella bacteria. It is one of the most common diseases to be known as food poisoning (though the name refers to food-borne illness in general).

Caused by a sudden burst of synchronized electrical activity in the brain, this neurological event affects roughly 50 million people worldwide and can range from a brief blank stare to a full convulsion — what is it?
Seizure: Period of symptoms due to excessive or synchronous neuronal brain activity.
This layer of tissue covering a vertebrate's body serves three main functions: protection, regulation, and sensation?
Skin: Soft outer covering organ of vertebrates.

First described in 1915 by a German paleontologist from Egyptian fossils that were destroyed during World War II, this dinosaur genus wasn't represented by new material until the early 2000s — which genus?
Spinosaurus: Genus of spinosaurid dinosaur. The genus was known first from Egyptian remains discovered in 1912 and described by German palaeontologist Ernst Stromer in 1915.

This small nocturnal marsupial has membranes stretching from its forelegs to hindlegs that let it soar between trees, and its scientific name translates to 'short-headed rope-dancer' — what animal is it?
Sugar glider: Species of Australian marsupial.
Nicknamed water bears and moss piglets, these eight-legged micro-animals shrug off extreme heat, crushing pressure, and even radiation. What are they?
This French economist's best-selling 2013 book argued that capital returns persistently outpace economic growth, driving ever-rising wealth inequality — who is he?
This passive, energy-free process moves water through a plant and releases it as vapor from its leaves, also cooling the plant and driving nutrient flow — what is it called?
Transpiration: Process of water movement through a plant. Transpiration is the process of water movement through a plant and its evaporation from aerial parts, such as leaves, stems and flowers.
Silvery-grey and sitting at atomic number 92, this actinide has the highest atomic weight of any element that occurs naturally on Earth — and its slow decay helps date the planet itself. What is it?
Uranium: Chemical element with atomic number 92 (U)

This Soviet cosmonaut commanded the first spaceflight to carry more than one crew member in 1964, then became the first human to die during a space mission when his parachute failed in 1967 — who was he?
Also called a slater or sow bug depending on region, this terrestrial crustacean is one of the few crustacean lineages to fully colonize dry land — what is it?
The symbol for chlorine is Cl. Chlorine is a chemical element; it has symbol Cl and atomic number 17.
The symbol for zirconium is Zr. Zirconium is a chemical element; it has symbol Zr and atomic number 40.
